strongest_case_for: Case 1 is the only problem statement where every input is fixed and public and every mark is explicit, and it is the only one for which this team already holds reproduced results before writing a single slide. Specifically: (a) the dataset is mandated, downloaded and ETag-verified on this machine (12.4 MB, no login) [verified_fact]; (b) a no-tuning scikit-learn HistGradientBoosting baseline with rolling features has been run on ALL FOUR subsets on this laptop, CPU-only, 1.2–3.5 min each, and independently re-run three more times, agreeing within 0.4 RMSE (FD001 test RMSE 14.2 capped / 15.4 raw, NASA score ≈310) [verified_fact]; (c) the PDF gives fourteen weighted criteria across two rounds, and in Round 2 75% of the weight (Working pipeline 20 + Data engineering quality 15 + MLOps in action 10 + Agent behavior 10 + Demo & explanation 20) rewards a complete, reproducible, explainable engineering loop rather than Model performance (15) [source_derived_requirement]; that is a backend/REST/DB/React team's home turf. (d) The PDF itself prescribes the Round 1 content (architecture diagram data→features→model→agent→work order; cleaning/feature approach; model choice with reasoning; Triage Agent logic) [source_derived_requirement], so the single slide the platform demands has a given skeleton. (e) The crowd competes on the wrong 15%: none of the 20 rendered `cmapss` topic repos (of 53) nor the one self-reported hackathon-winner repo mentions MLflow, drift, retraining or a triage agent [verified_fact for the search; technical_inference for the conclusion]; the closed loop the rubric scores (interval-lower-bound triage, drift-gated promotion with accept AND reject, four-subset coverage, leakage audit, decision-replay of the agent as a maintenance policy) is what no public C-MAPSS repo found provides. (f) Zero environmental dependency on root, kernel modules, ARM hardware, GPU, paid APIs or a lab; the whole stack resolves in pip (pandas 2.x pinned, MLflow 3 on SQLite with aliases, Evidently 0.7.23, Streamlit with pinned plotly) [verified_fact]. (g) It ranked first under all four weighting schemes, all four input views, both blind judges and all three adversarial reviewers (7.86 risk-adjusted vs Case 3's 7.26) [verified_fact about the prior analysis]. Under the real format (deck-first, prototype as annex, one slide in six days, four-week Round 2 window) the value of a case whose evidence is already in hand and whose evidence is tables rather than live hardware demos goes UP, not down.
round1_single_slide_plan:
WHAT THE PLATFORM SAYS (new fact, platform-level): the Unstop listing says "Submit a single slide (PDF format) on that problem statement only" and "Assessors and a jury shortlist the top entries"; it specifies NO slide content, NO file-size limit and NO criteria [verified_fact, platform-level]. So the only content spec that exists is the Case 1 PDF's own Round 1 list (four items) and its seven weighted criteria [source_derived_requirement]. Assessors reading hundreds of one-pagers will, in my inference, scan for: all four PDF-named items present; one legible diagram; specific choices with one-line reasons; and anything concrete that proves the team can execute [technical_inference]. The slide must be readable at thumbnail scale; a wall of text loses Architecture clarity (20%) and Communication quality (5%) at once.

THE SLIDE (16:9, one page, exported to PDF, fonts embedded, under 5 MB per the Season 3 precedent [unverified_assumption]):
- Title band (1 line): "SentinelLoop: drift-gated, uncertainty-aware prognostics that raise work orders from the RUL lower bound and escalate only exceptions." Reuses the PDF's words (closed loop, RUL, work order, human for exceptions) → Problem understanding 15%.
- Centre, ~45% of area: ONE architecture diagram following the PDF's exact chain: C-MAPSS batch/stream replay → clean (per-unit forward-fill, EMA, sensor drop list, train-only KMeans-6 regimes + per-regime scaling) → rolling mean/std/slope W=20 → [IsolationForest anomaly | HGBR RUL cap-125 | CQR 90% interval] → Triage Agent → work order (SQLite/JSON). Side loop drawn in a second colour: Evidently feature drift → retrain job → promotion gate → MLflow registry (SQLite, champion/challenger aliases) → dashboard. → Architecture clarity 20%.
- Left strip (Data engineering 15%): five bullets, each with a reason, including "engine-level GroupKFold with random truncation; preprocessing fit on train only" and the proof line "naive last-cycle validation gives RMSE 2.5, the real test gives 14.2: we evaluate the honest way" [verified_fact].
- Right strip (ML approach & reasoning 20%): IsolationForest on healthy windows (handles the 'mild imbalance' ground rule explicitly, explainable); HGBR + conformalized quantile intervals (cite Robinson, IJPHM 2026: 88–92% coverage at 90% nominal); one line on why not LSTM/transformer (15% weight on accuracy, +1–2 RMSE only, explainability, CPU retraining in minutes during a demo); a logged deep challenger for comparison.
- Bottom-left (MLOps & agent logic 15%): a 5-row severity rule table on rul_lower / anomaly / drift / interval width → CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, WATCH, ESCALATE_TO_HUMAN, plus "one open order per engine" and "gate: challenger promoted only if validation RMSE and coverage do not regress".
- Bottom-right (Dataset coverage 10%): "All four subsets through configuration; regimes for FD002/FD004, dual fault modes for FD003/FD004" and the proof strip: "Already running on a CPU laptop: test RMSE 14.2 / 16.2 / 14.1 / 17.9 (capped), 1–4 min per subset" [verified_fact]. That line is the single most differentiating element a Round 1 assessor can see: a plan with numbers already behind it.
- Footer: tools (Python, scikit-learn, MLflow, Evidently, Streamlit; no LLM) and the Saxena PHM08 citation.

CAN IT BE DONE IN SIX DAYS? Yes, with margin. Every content element already exists in the prior report (Section D architecture, agent rule table, stack table, validation table) and the numbers are reproduced [verified_fact]. The new work is layout and compression: day 1–2 draft in PowerPoint/Figma-free tools, day 3 readability test (phone screen, a non-team reader must say what the system does in 20 s), day 4 second version with the diagram simplified, day 5 PDF export and size check, day 6 buffer and portal upload by the team leader. In parallel, run the existing baseline script from a clean clone on every teammate's machine so the numbers on the slide are the team's own run [technical_inference]. Main risk is over-density; mitigation is a hard rule of one diagram, two strips, two tables, one proof line, nothing else.

rubric_outcome_estimate:
Official weights exist for both rounds of Case 1 (fourteen criteria, exact names and weights as printed in the PDF) [source_derived_requirement]; Case 3's PDF publishes criteria without weights (per the prior report), so its outcome is an unweighted mean. Estimates below start from the prior report's three-evaluator means and are adjusted by me for the now-known single-slide and deck-first format [technical_inference throughout].

ROUND 1 (one slide), weighted target ≈ 7.9 / 10:
- Problem understanding (15%): 8.3. Closed-loop framing, 'human for exceptions', explicit imbalance treatment, verified dataset facts.
- Architecture clarity (20%): 8.0 (down from 8.2 for compression risk). One diagram in the PDF's exact chain with the MLOps side loop; the format rewards a case whose architecture is a linear pipeline.
- Data engineering approach (15%): 7.8. Train-only regime handling, drop list, rolling features, engine-level splits, the 2.5-vs-14.2 proof line.
- ML approach & reasoning (20%): 7.8. GBM + CQR + IsolationForest justified against the 15% accuracy weight and explainability; Robinson 2026 cited; flagged Hard by both blind judges because the ML is not novel.
- MLOps & agent logic (15%): 8.0. Rule table and gated retraining fit in two small tables.
- Dataset coverage (10%): 7.7. Four-subset plan with regime and dual-fault handling, plus already-measured four-subset numbers; Hard because FD002/FD004 are genuinely harder.
- Communication quality (5%): 7.5 (down from 8.0 for density risk on one slide).

ROUND 2 (10 slides + annex), weighted target ≈ 7.8 / 10:
- Working pipeline (20%): 8.3. `make demo` from a clean clone, lock file, Docker, pytest, offline; recorded run for judges who never execute code.
- Data engineering quality (15%): 7.8. Seeds, schema checks, feature manifest, train-only preprocessing.
- Model performance (15%): 7.2 (Hard). Baseline 14.2/16.2/14.1/17.9 capped and 15.4/27.9/15.7/28.9 raw [verified_fact] is in the published classical band but 2–3 RMSE above deep models on FD001; the 'sensibly interpreted' half (both RMSEs, PHM08 convention, PICP) is where the marks come from.
- MLOps in action (10%): 7.8. Alias-based registry on SQLite, drift-triggered retrain, gate accept AND reject.
- Agent behavior (10%): 8.3. Unit-tested rule table on the lower bound, confusion matrix, de-duplication, escalation measured.
- Dataset coverage (10%): 7.7 (Hard). Four-subset results table.
- Demo & explanation (20%): 7.7 (Hard, one judge). Deck-first format makes this the biggest variable: the policy-replay table, gate log and honest-metrics slide must do the work the live demo would otherwise do; the roadmap slide answers the platform's 'implementation roadmap' ask.

Where no weights exist: Case 3 (and Cases 4, 5) have none, so for those only an unweighted mean can be stated; the prior report puts Case 3 at ≈7.2 unweighted with two criteria flagged Hard.
honest_weaknesses:
1. Most crowded, most templated problem of the five: 53 `cmapss` repos and 217 `remaining-useful-life` repos exist [verified_fact]; a judge who wants a visibly new idea can score the ML as a competent reproduction. The ML design (GBM + CQR) is published (Robinson 2026) and must be cited, not claimed. Our differentiators are integration- and honesty-level, which is exactly what is hardest to make visible on ONE slide; the thing that wins Round 2 (policy replay, drift gate) may read as 'MLOps hygiene' to a tired Round 1 assessor [technical_inference].
2. If Case 1 attracts the largest and most ML-capable pool and shortlisting is relative within each case, our Round 1 margin narrows; nothing is known about pool size per case [unverified_assumption / hypothesis].
3. Model performance is capped: 14.2 on FD001 vs 11–13 for tuned deep models; FD002/FD004 RMSE against raw truth stays ≈28 [verified_fact]. A team that tunes a transformer may post a lower headline number, and a judge who weights that number will prefer them.
4. Environment fragility was observed on this very machine (LightGBM access violation; Streamlit import failure from a plotly mismatch; pandas 3.0 pulled by an unpinned install) [verified_fact]. Pinning fixes it, but a 40%-weight pipeline-plus-demo rubric punishes any slip.
5. Capacity: the prior estimates assumed 3–4 people; this team is 2–3. Claude Max compensates for code volume, not for the time to learn MLflow 3 aliases and Evidently 0.7 semantics; the skeptic's 14–18 person-days is the planning figure [technical_inference].
6. Work done between 25 Oct and 14 Nov is wasted if the team is not shortlisted; the shortlist date is unknown [unverified_assumption]. Same for every case, but Case 1's plan front-loads more of it.
7. Interpretive risks: 'mild imbalance' is odd for regression and must be addressed explicitly as severity-class imbalance or it looks ignored; the PDF says 'Design deck' for Round 1 while the platform says one slide, so the four PDF items must be compressed and no official guidance says how.
8. Inherent limits to state openly: C-MAPSS is simulated with one snapshot per cycle; streaming is replay; residual drift cannot be computed live without labels; no real CMMS; conformal coverage is subset-dependent (0.84–0.95 in the literature) and the headline 88–92% is a single-run figure [verified_fact].
9. Case 3's counter-argument is real: a 638 → 41 ms loaded-RTT plot [verified_fact, measured once] is more memorable than RMSE 14.2 on a benchmark with 53 repos; its field is probably thinner; its PDF prescribes the evidence format. If judges reward dramatic, hard-to-fake measurements over rubric completeness, or if a teammate turns out to have Linux tc/netem fluency, all three adversarial reviewers would pick Case 3 and the dimension model calls it a toss-up.
10. The IP clause ('exclusive property of Tata Elxsi') applies to whatever we submit; it is not a differential weakness but the team should know it before investing eight weeks.

why_this_beats_the_other:
Under the ACTUAL format (one slide in six days; a 10-slide deck plus annex in a four-week window; a finale presentation to senior leaders; judges who may never run code), four things decide it for THIS team:

1. The slide writes itself and already has numbers. Case 1's PDF names the four Round 1 items and seven weighted criteria [source_derived_requirement]; the architecture, rule table and stack are drafted; the four-subset baseline is reproduced on this laptop [verified_fact]. In six days the team can submit a slide whose proof strip says 'already running: 14.2 / 16.2 / 14.1 / 17.9'. Case 3's slide would have to explain Linux traffic control, a flow classifier, capacity estimation and a verify-or-rollback actuator to assessors with no weights to guide them, backed by one measurement the team did not make and cannot yet confidently extend (the skeptic ran the WSL2 testbed once; nobody on the team has tc/netem fluency) [verified_fact for the measurement; technical_inference for the rest].

2. Evidence that fits a deck beats evidence that needs a testbed. With the prototype as an annex, what scores is what fits on slides and can be re-derived by a reader: per-subset RMSE tables, PICP, a gate log, a policy-replay table, all from public data via `pip install` [technical_inference]. Case 3's evidence is a latency plot whose credibility rests on a root-and-kernel-dependent namespace testbed with 40 ms idle spikes on WSL2 and no CAKE [verified_fact]; a judge cannot reproduce it from the deck and the team cannot easily defend its stability criterion.

3. Skill fit and variance in a four-week window. Case 1 skill-fit 9 vs Case 3 6.0 (joint-lowest) in the prior analysis; the failure modes of Case 1 are pip-level (pin and rehearse), those of Case 3 are kernel-level and silent [verified_fact for the observed failures]. With 2–3 students and a hard 13 Dec close, the lowest-variance path is worth more than a higher 'wow' ceiling. Every reviewer's stated flip condition (a demonstrated Linux-networking teammate) is absent.

4. The finale story. 'A fleet of trucks streams sensor data; the model predicts remaining life with an honest uncertainty band; the agent raises a work order from the lower bound and escalates only exceptions; the system notices drift and retrains itself, and refuses a worse model' is a narrative senior Tata Elxsi leaders in transportation and industrial practices can follow without networking background, and it carries two memorable moments (the 2.5-vs-14.2 leakage trap; the gate rejecting a challenger). I concede Case 3's 638 → 41 ms is the more dramatic single number; the counter is that Case 1 has three or four checkable numbers per slide and a rubric that rewards exactly that.

Net: Case 1 won every weighting scheme, both blind judges and all three adversarial reviewers (7.86 vs 7.26) BEFORE the format was known; the format now known (deck-first, annexed prototype, six-day first deadline) favours the case with prescribed content, explicit weights, public data and already-reproduced results. The honest exception stands: if a teammate has real Linux tc/netem experience, or the judges demonstrably reward dramatic measurements over rubric completeness, Case 3 becomes a genuine toss-up; neither condition is known to hold today.
